# Process Scheduling Fundamentals

## Why CPU scheduling is needed
In a multiprogrammed system several processes are kept in memory at the same time. When the running process has to wait (usually for I/O), the operating system takes the CPU away from it and gives it to another process. The goal is to keep the CPU busy as much as possible. Choosing which ready process gets the CPU next is called CPU scheduling or process scheduling.

## CPU burst and I/O burst cycle
Process execution alternates between CPU bursts (computing) and I/O bursts (waiting for devices). A process starts and ends with a CPU burst. Most CPU bursts are short and only a few are long. An I/O-bound process has many short CPU bursts, while a CPU-bound process has a few long CPU bursts. This distribution matters when choosing a scheduling algorithm.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

text:
rocess has many short CPU bursts, while a CPU-bound process has a few long CPU bursts. This distribution matters when choosing a scheduling algorithm.

## Process states and queues
A process moves between the states new, ready, running, waiting (blocked) and terminated. Processes that are in memory and ready to run wait in the ready queue. Processes waiting for an I/O device wait in a device queue. The scheduler selects processes only from the ready queue.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

## Types of schedulers
- Long-term scheduler (job scheduler): decides which jobs are admitted into memory. It controls the degree of multiprogramming and runs infrequently.
- Short-term scheduler (CPU scheduler): selects which ready process runs next on the CPU. It runs very often (every few milliseconds), so it must be fast.
- Medium-term scheduler: swaps processes out of memory and later back in, to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or improve the process mix.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

- Medium-term scheduler: swaps processes out of memory and later back in, to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or improve the process mix.

## Dispatcher
The dispatcher is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler. It performs the context switch, switches to user mode, and jumps to the proper location in the user program. The time it takes to stop one process and start another is called dispatch latency. A context switch saves the state (PCB) of the old process and loads the saved state of the new one. Context-switch time is pure overhead because no useful work is done during it.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

tate (PCB) of the old process and loads the saved state of the new one. Context-switch time is pure overhead because no useful work is done during it.

## When scheduling decisions happen
Scheduling decisions can take place when a process:
1. switches from running to waiting (for example, an I/O request),
2. switches from running to ready (for example, a timer interrupt),
3. switches from waiting to ready (for example, I/O completion),
4. terminates.

If scheduling happens only in cases 1 and 4, the scheme is non-preemptive (cooperative): once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it blocks or terminates. If scheduling can also happen in cases 2 and 3, the scheme is preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away from a running process.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

## Preemptive vs non-preemptive
Non-preemptive scheduling is simple and has low overhead, but a long process can hold the CPU and make short or interactive processes wait. Preemptive scheduling gives better response time for interactive systems, but costs extra context switches and can cause race conditions on shared data, which needs synchronisation. FCFS, SJF and non-preemptive Priority are non-preemptive. SRTF, preemptive Priority and Round Robin are preemptive.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

## Thread scheduling
On systems that support threads, the kernel schedules kernel-level threads, not processes. With process-contention scope (PCS), the thread library schedules user threads onto available LWPs, and competition is among threads of the same process. With system-contention scope (SCS), the kernel decides which kernel thread runs, and competition is among all threads in the system.
source: Scheduling fundamentals

# Scheduling Criteria and Performance Measures

## Criteria used to compare algorithms
- CPU utilisation: the percentage of time the CPU is busy. Should be maximised.
- Throughput: the number of processes completed per unit time. Should be maximised.
- Turnaround time: the total time from submission (arrival) to completion of a process. Should be minimised.
- Waiting time: the total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue. The scheduling algorithm directly affects only this. Should be minimised.
- Response time: the time from submission until the process first gets the CPU (first response). Important for interactive systems. Should be minimised.

Usually we optimise the average value. For interactive systems it can be more important to minimise the variance of response time than the average.
source: Scheduling criteria

text:
.

Usually we optimise the average value. For interactive systems it can be more important to minimise the variance of response time than the average.

## Formulas (course convention)
- Arrival Time (AT): when the process enters the ready queue.
- Burst Time (BT): the CPU time the process needs.
- Completion Time (CT): when the process finishes, read from the Gantt chart.
- Turnaround Time: TAT = CT − AT
- Waiting Time: WT = TAT − BT
- Response Time: RT = (time the process first gets the CPU) − AT
- Average TAT = sum of all TAT ÷ number of processes. Average WT is found the same way.
- Throughput = number of processes ÷ total time span of the schedule.
- CPU utilisation = time the CPU is busy ÷ total time span × 100%.
source: Scheduling criteria

text:

- Throughput = number of processes ÷ total time span of the schedule.
- CPU utilisation = time the CPU is busy ÷ total time span × 100%.

## Common mistakes
- Writing TAT = CT and forgetting to subtract the arrival time. TAT = CT only when AT = 0.
- Writing WT = CT − BT. This is only correct when AT = 0. Always compute WT = TAT − BT.
- In preemptive algorithms, WT is not just "start time − arrival time". A preempted process waits again every time it is taken off the CPU, and WT = TAT − BT counts all of these waits. Start time − arrival time is the response time.
- Forgetting idle time. If no process has arrived, the CPU is idle. Show it as IDLE in the Gantt chart and do not count it as waiting for any process.
- Dividing by the wrong number of processes when averaging.
source: Scheduling criteria

## Gantt chart
A Gantt chart is a bar showing which process runs in each time interval, with the times written below the boundaries. Example: | P1 | P2 | P3 | with times 0, 5, 8, 16. The completion time of a process is the end of its last bar.
source: Scheduling criteria

# CPU Scheduling Algorithms

Course conventions: a lower priority number means higher priority. Ties are broken by earlier arrival time, then by lower process number. In Round Robin, a process arriving at the same moment a quantum expires joins the ready queue before the preempted process.

## First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
The process that requests the CPU first gets it first. It is implemented with a FIFO queue and is non-preemptive. It is simple, but the average waiting time is often long and depends heavily on arrival order.

Convoy effect: when one long CPU-bound process holds the CPU, many short I/O-bound processes wait behind it, like cars stuck behind a slow truck. Both CPU and device utilisation drop. FCFS is unsuitable for time-sharing systems.
source: Scheduling algorithms

text:

Worked example (FCFS): P1 (AT 0, BT 5), P2 (AT 1, BT 3), P3 (AT 2, BT 8), P4 (AT 3, BT 6).
Gantt chart: P1 [0-5] | P2 [5-8] | P3 [8-16] | P4 [16-22].
CT: P1 = 5, P2 = 8, P3 = 16, P4 = 22. TAT: 5, 7, 14, 19. WT: 0, 4, 6, 13.
Average TAT = 11.25, Average WT = 5.75.
source: Scheduling algorithms

text:
| P2 [5-8] | P3 [8-16] | P4 [16-22].
CT: P1 = 5, P2 = 8, P3 = 16, P4 = 22. TAT: 5, 7, 14, 19. WT: 0, 4, 6, 13.
Average TAT = 11.25, Average WT = 5.75.

## Shortest Job First (SJF), non-preemptive
When the CPU becomes free, it is given to the arrived process with the smallest next CPU burst. SJF is provably optimal: it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes, because moving a short process before a long one reduces the short one's wait more than it increases the long one's wait. Its difficulty is that the length of the next CPU burst is not known in advance. It is predicted with exponential averaging: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n), where t(n) is the actual length of the nth burst, τ(n) is the past prediction, and 0 ≤ α ≤ 1 (commonly α = 1/2). Long processes can starve if short ones keep arriving.
source: Scheduling algorithms

Key rule: choose only among processes that have already arrived. A short job that has not arrived yet cannot be chosen.

Worked example (SJF): P1 (AT 0, BT 7), P2 (AT 2, BT 4), P3 (AT 4, BT 1), P4 (AT 5, BT 4).
At time 0 only P1 has arrived, so it runs to completion: P1 [0-7]. At 7, P2, P3 and P4 are ready, so P3 (BT 1) runs: P3 [7-8]. P2 and P4 tie at BT 4, and P2 arrived first: P2 [8-12], then P4 [12-16].
CT: P1 = 7, P2 = 12, P3 = 8, P4 = 16. TAT: 7, 10, 4, 11. WT: 0, 6, 3, 7.
Average TAT = 8.00, Average WT = 4.00.

CT: P1 = 7, P2 = 12, P3 = 8, P4 = 16. TAT: 7, 10, 4, 11. WT: 0, 6, 3, 7.
Average TAT = 8.00, Average WT = 4.00.

## Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), preemptive SJF
Whenever a new process arrives, the scheduler compares its burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the new process needs less time, the running process is preempted. SRTF gives a lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF but causes more context switches.

Worked example (SRTF) with the same processes: P1 (0, 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4).
P1 runs 0-2. At 2, P2 (4) < P1 remaining (5), so P2 preempts and runs 2-4. At 4, P3 (1) < P2 remaining (2), so P3 runs 4-5. At 5, P2 remaining 2 is the smallest, so P2 runs 5-7. Then P4 (4) < P1 (5), so P4 runs 7-11. Finally P1 runs 11-16.
Gantt chart: P1 [0-2] | P2 [2-4] | P3 [4-5] | P2 [5-7] | P4 [7-11] | P1 [11-16].
CT: P1 = 16, P2 = 7, P3 = 5, P4 = 11. TAT: 16, 5, 1, 6. WT: 9, 1, 0, 2.
Average TAT = 7.00, Average WT = 3.00. Note that P1's waiting time (9) is the sum of all the time it spent preempted.

Average TAT = 7.00, Average WT = 3.00. Note that P1's waiting time (9) is the sum of all the time it spent preempted.

## Priority Scheduling
Each process has a priority and the CPU goes to the highest-priority ready process (lowest number, in this course). SJF is a special case where the priority is the predicted next burst. Priority scheduling can be non-preemptive or preemptive. In the preemptive version, a newly arrived process with higher priority preempts the running one.

Starvation (indefinite blocking): low-priority processes may never run if higher-priority ones keep arriving. Aging solves this by gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait a long time.

Gantt chart: P1 [0-4] | P2 [4-7] | P4 [7-12] | P3 [12-14]. WT: P1 0, P2 3, P3 10, P4 4. Average WT = 4.25, Average TAT = 7.75.

## Round Robin (RR)
Designed for time-sharing. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue. Each process gets the CPU for at most one time quantum q. If it has not finished when the quantum expires, it is preempted and put at the tail of the ready queue. If its burst is shorter than q, it releases the CPU voluntarily. With n processes, no process waits more than (n − 1)·q before its next quantum, so response time is good.
source: Scheduling algorithms

Choosing the quantum: if q is very large, RR becomes FCFS. If q is very small, there are too many context switches and overhead dominates. A rule of thumb is that about 80% of CPU bursts should be shorter than q. q must also be large compared to the context-switch time. Average turnaround time does not necessarily improve as q increases.

P1 runs 0-2. P2 (arrived 1) and P3 (arrived 2) join before the preempted P1, so the queue is P2, P3, P1. P2 runs 2-4; P4 arrives at 4 and joins before P2, so the queue is P3, P1, P4, P2. P3 runs 4-6 and finishes. P1 runs 6-8, P4 runs 8-9 and finishes, P2 runs 9-11 and finishes, P1 runs 11-12 and finishes.
Gantt chart: P1 [0-2] | P2 [2-4] | P3 [4-6] | P1 [6-8] | P4 [8-9] | P2 [9-11] | P1 [11-12].

## Comparison summary
- FCFS: simple, non-preemptive, convoy effect, poor for interactive use.
- SJF: optimal average waiting time, needs burst prediction, long jobs can starve.
- SRTF: preemptive SJF, even lower average waiting time, more context switches.
- Priority: flexible, risk of starvation, fixed by aging.
- Round Robin: fair, good response time, performance depends on the quantum, higher average turnaround than SJF.
source: Scheduling algorithms

# Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-Time Scheduling

## Multilevel Queue Scheduling
The ready queue is split into several separate queues, for example foreground (interactive) and background (batch). Each process is permanently assigned to one queue based on a property such as process type or memory size. Each queue has its own algorithm, for example RR for foreground and FCFS for background. Scheduling between queues is usually fixed-priority preemptive (background runs only when foreground is empty, which risks starvation) or time-sliced (for example, 80% of CPU time to foreground and 20% to background). A typical order from highest priority is: system processes, interactive processes, interactive editing processes, batch processes, student processes.
source: Advanced scheduling

text:
A typical order from highest priority is: system processes, interactive processes, interactive editing processes, batch processes, student processes.

## Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
Like a multilevel queue, but processes can move between queues. A process that uses too much CPU time is moved to a lower-priority queue, so I/O-bound and interactive processes stay in the higher queues. A process that waits too long in a low queue can be moved up, which is aging and prevents starvation. Example: queue 0 is RR with q = 8, queue 1 is RR with q = 16, queue 2 is FCFS. A new process enters queue 0. If it does not finish within 8 ms it moves to queue 1, and if it still does not finish within 16 more ms it moves to queue 2. An MLFQ is defined by the number of queues, the algorithm for each queue, the rules for upgrading and demoting processes, and the rule for which queue a new process enters. It is the most general scheme but also the most complex to configure.
source: Advanced scheduling

## Multiprocessor Scheduling
- Asymmetric multiprocessing: one master processor makes all scheduling decisions and the others run only user code. This is simple because only one processor accesses system data structures.
- Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP): each processor schedules itself, from a common ready queue or from a private per-processor queue.
- Processor affinity: a process tends to stay on the processor where it has been running, because that processor's cache already holds its data. Soft affinity is a preference; hard affinity is a guarantee.
- Load balancing: keeps the workload evenly spread. With push migration, a task periodically moves processes from overloaded processors to idle ones. With pull migration, an idle processor pulls a waiting task from a busy one. Load balancing works against processor affinity.
- Multicore and hardware threads: when a core stalls on a memory
source: Advanced scheduling

text:

- Multicore and hardware threads: when a core stalls on a memory access, it can switch to another hardware thread, so scheduling happens at two levels.
source: Advanced scheduling

text:
Multicore and hardware threads: when a core stalls on a memory access, it can switch to another hardware thread, so scheduling happens at two levels.

## Real-Time Scheduling
- Soft real-time systems give critical tasks preference but do not guarantee deadlines. Hard real-time systems must meet deadlines.
- Real-time processes are often periodic, with processing time t, deadline d and period p, where 0 ≤ t ≤ d ≤ p.
- Rate-Monotonic Scheduling: static priorities, where a shorter period gets a higher priority. It is optimal among static-priority schemes. CPU utilisation is bounded by N(2^(1/N) − 1), about 69% for large N.
- Earliest Deadline First (EDF): dynamic priorities, where the earlier deadline gets the higher priority. In theory it can reach 100% CPU utilisation.
- Real-time scheduling needs preemptive, priority-based scheduling and low interrupt and dispatch latency.
source: Advanced scheduling

text:
n theory it can reach 100% CPU utilisation.
- Real-time scheduling needs preemptive, priority-based scheduling and low interrupt and dispatch latency.

## Examples from real operating systems
- Linux uses the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), which tracks each task's virtual runtime and runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime, stored in a red-black tree. Nice values weight how fast virtual runtime grows. Linux also has real-time classes (SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR) with higher priority than normal tasks.
- Windows uses a preemptive, priority-based scheduler with 32 priority levels. The highest-priority ready thread runs, and interactive threads get priority boosts.
source: Advanced scheduling

# Process Scheduling Viva and Exam Question Bank

Q: Differentiate between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling.
A: In non-preemptive scheduling, a running process keeps the CPU until it terminates or blocks for I/O. In preemptive scheduling, the OS can take the CPU away, for example on a timer interrupt or when a higher-priority process arrives. Preemptive scheduling improves responsiveness but adds context-switch overhead and needs synchronisation for shared data.

Q: What is the difference between the scheduler and the dispatcher?
A: The short-term scheduler decides which ready process runs next. The dispatcher carries out that decision: it switches context, switches to user mode, and jumps to the right instruction. Dispatch latency is the dispatcher's overhead.
source: Viva question bank

text:
ries out that decision: it switches context, switches to user mode, and jumps to the right instruction. Dispatch latency is the dispatcher's overhead.

Q: Why is SJF called optimal, and why is it hard to implement?
A: For a given set of processes it gives the minimum average waiting time, because running shorter jobs first reduces total waiting. It is hard to implement because the next CPU burst length is unknown, so it must be predicted, for example by exponential averaging.

Q: What is the convoy effect?
A: In FCFS, short processes stuck behind one long process all wait, which lowers CPU and I/O device utilisation.

Q: What is starvation and how is it solved?
A: Starvation is when a low-priority process waits indefinitely because higher-priority processes keep getting the CPU. Aging solves it by gradually raising the priority of processes that have waited a long time.
source: Viva question bank

text:

Q: How does the time quantum affect Round Robin?
A: A very large quantum makes RR behave like FCFS. A very small quantum causes too many context switches and high overhead. The quantum should be large compared to the context-switch time, and about 80% of CPU bursts should finish within one quantum.

Q: What is the difference between turnaround time, waiting time and response time?
A: Turnaround time is completion minus arrival (the total time in the system). Waiting time is the total time spent in the ready queue (TAT − BT). Response time is the time until the process first gets the CPU.
source: Viva question bank

Q: Which algorithms can cause starvation?
A: SJF, SRTF and Priority scheduling (and fixed-priority multilevel queues). FCFS and Round Robin do not cause starvation.

Q: How is a multilevel feedback queue different from a multilevel queue?
A: In a multilevel queue, processes are permanently assigned to one queue. In a multilevel feedback queue, processes move between queues based on their CPU usage, and aging moves long-waiting processes up.

Q: What is processor affinity?
A: It is the tendency to keep a process on the same processor to reuse its warm cache. Soft affinity is a preference and hard affinity is a strict binding. Load balancing can conflict with it.

Q: Is SRTF always better than SJF?
A: It gives an equal or lower average waiting time, but it causes more context switches, needs burst-length prediction, and can starve long processes more severely.

Q: What is a CPU-bound process versus an I/O-bound process?
A: A CPU-bound process spends most of its time computing and has long CPU bursts. An I/O-bound process does a lot of I/O and has many short CPU bursts. A good scheduler mixes both to keep the CPU and the devices busy.

# How to Create a Gantt Chart and Solve a Scheduling Problem

## What a Gantt chart is
A Gantt chart for CPU scheduling is a horizontal timeline that shows which process is using the CPU during each interval of time. Each box is labelled with a process name, and the time at each box boundary is written underneath. Example:
| P1 | P2 | P3 |
0    5    8    16
This means P1 ran from 0 to 5, P2 from 5 to 8 and P3 from 8 to 16. If no process is ready, the CPU is idle and the box is labelled IDLE.
source: Gantt chart guide

text:
5    8    16
This means P1 ran from 0 to 5, P2 from 5 to 8 and P3 from 8 to 16. If no process is ready, the CPU is idle and the box is labelled IDLE.

## The general method (works for every algorithm)
1. Write the process table: process, arrival time (AT), burst time (BT), and priority if given.
2. Start the clock at the earliest arrival time.
3. At every decision point, list the ready queue: all processes that have arrived (AT ≤ current time) and are not finished.
4. Apply the algorithm's rule to pick one process from the ready queue.
5. Decide how long it runs. In non-preemptive algorithms it runs until it finishes. In preemptive algorithms it runs until it finishes OR until a new arrival might preempt it. In Round Robin it runs for at most one time quantum.
6. Draw that box on the timeline, move the clock forward, and repeat from step 3 until every process is finished.
7. If the ready queue is empty, draw an IDLE box until the next arrival.
source: Gantt chart guide

text:
ve the clock forward, and repeat from step 3 until every process is finished.
7. If the ready queue is empty, draw an IDLE box until the next arrival.

## Decision points for each algorithm
- FCFS: pick the earliest arrival. Decision points are only when a process finishes.
- SJF (non-preemptive): pick the smallest burst time among processes that have ALREADY arrived. Decide only when a process finishes.
- SRTF: pick the smallest remaining time. Re-check at every arrival and at every completion, because a new short process can preempt the running one.
- Priority non-preemptive: pick the highest priority (lowest number) among arrived processes when the CPU becomes free.
- Priority preemptive: same rule, but re-check at every arrival; a higher-priority arrival preempts the running process.
- Round Robin: take the process at the front of the ready queue and run it for at most q units. If it is not finished, put it at the back of the queue, after any processes that arrived during its quantum.
source: Gantt chart guide

text:
ady queue and run it for at most q units. If it is not finished, put it at the back of the queue, after any processes that arrived during its quantum.

## Solving: from the Gantt chart to the answers
1. Completion Time (CT): the time at the right edge of the LAST box of that process.
2. Turnaround Time: TAT = CT − AT.
3. Waiting Time: WT = TAT − BT. This automatically counts every period the process spent waiting, including after preemptions.
4. Response Time: RT = (start of the FIRST box of that process) − AT.
5. Averages: add the column and divide by the number of processes.
6. Check your work: the sum of all burst times plus idle time must equal the total length of the Gantt chart, and no WT can be negative.
source: Gantt chart guide

text:

6. Check your work: the sum of all burst times plus idle time must equal the total length of the Gantt chart, and no WT can be negative.

## Worked example (FCFS)
Processes: P1 (AT 0, BT 4), P2 (AT 1, BT 3), P3 (AT 2, BT 1).
At t=0 only P1 is ready, so P1 runs 0 to 4. At t=4 P2 and P3 are waiting; P2 arrived first, so P2 runs 4 to 7. Then P3 runs 7 to 8.
Gantt chart: | P1 | P2 | P3 | with times 0, 4, 7, 8.
CT: P1 = 4, P2 = 7, P3 = 8. TAT: 4 − 0 = 4, 7 − 1 = 6, 8 − 2 = 6. WT: 4 − 4 = 0, 6 − 3 = 3, 6 − 1 = 5.
Average TAT = 16 / 3 = 5.33. Average WT = 8 / 3 = 2.67.
Notice that P3 needed only 1 unit but waited 5. This is the convoy effect, and it is exactly why SJF was invented: with SJF, P3 would run at t=4 and wait only 2.
source: Gantt chart guide

text:
P3 needed only 1 unit but waited 5. This is the convoy effect, and it is exactly why SJF was invented: with SJF, P3 would run at t=4 and wait only 2.

## Typical exam mistakes when drawing Gantt charts
- Choosing a process that has not arrived yet (for example, picking the shortest job in SJF even though it arrives later).
- Forgetting to re-check for preemption at every arrival in SRTF and preemptive Priority.
- In Round Robin, putting the preempted process back in the queue before the processes that arrived during its quantum.
- Forgetting idle time when no process has arrived.
- Reading the start of a box as the completion time.
source: Gantt chart guide

# Introduction, OS Structure, System Calls and Interrupts

## What an operating system is
An operating system (OS) is the program that manages the computer's hardware and provides services to application programs. Two standard views:
- Resource allocator: it decides how the CPU, memory, storage and devices are shared between programs and users, fairly and efficiently.
- Control program: it supervises programs so that errors and misuse do not harm the system.

Goals of an operating system: convenience for the user, efficient use of the hardware, and the ability to evolve (new hardware and services can be added without rewriting everything).

A computer system has four components: the hardware (CPU, memory, I/O devices), the operating system, application programs, and users.

## Kernel and shell
- The kernel is the core of the OS. It is the one program that runs at all times; it manages processes, memory, files and devices.
- The shell is a user program that reads commands and asks the kernel to carry them out (bash and zsh on Linux). It is the user's interface to the kernel; it is not part of the kernel.

## Dual-mode operation
The CPU has a mode bit: kernel mode (0) and user mode (1). Privileged instructions (I/O, changing the timer, managing interrupts, changing memory protection) can only run in kernel mode. User programs run in user mode; when they need a service, they make a system call, which switches the CPU to kernel mode, runs the kernel code, and switches back. A timer interrupt makes sure the OS regains control even from a program stuck in a loop.

## Operating system structures
- Monolithic: the whole kernel is one large program in one address space (traditional UNIX; Linux). Fast, because calls between parts are ordinary function calls, but a bug anywhere can crash the system and it is hard to maintain.
- Layered: the OS is split into layers; each layer uses only the services of the layers below it. Easy to debug, but hard to define the layers and slower because a request passes through many layers.
- Microkernel: only the essentials (inter-process communication, basic scheduling, low-level memory management) stay in the kernel; file systems, drivers and so on run as user-space servers that communicate by message passing (Mach, QNX). More reliable and secure, but message passing adds overhead.
- Modular: a core kernel plus loadable kernel modules that can be added at run time (Linux modules, Solaris). Combines the speed of monoli
source: OS structure and system calls

text:

- Modular: a core kernel plus loadable kernel modules that can be added at run time (Linux modules, Solaris). Combines the speed of monolithic kernels with flexibility.
- Hybrid: a mix of the above (Windows; macOS and iOS with the XNU kernel, which combines Mach with BSD code).

## Key abstractions
The OS hides hardware details behind abstractions: the process (a running program), virtual memory (each process sees its own large address space), the file (named persistent data), devices (uniform interfaces to hardware), and threads (units of execution inside a process).

## System calls
A system call is the programming interface to the services of the OS: a controlled way for a user program to ask the kernel to do something it is not allowed to do itself.

Life cycle of a system call:
1. The program calls a library wrapper function, for example `read()` in the C library.
2. The wrapper puts the system-call number and the parameters in agreed places and executes a trap instruction.
3. The trap switches the CPU to kernel mode and jumps to the system-call handler.
4. The handler looks the number up in the system-call table and runs the matching kernel function.
5. The result is placed in a register, the CPU returns to user mode, and the wrapper returns the value.

Parameter passing: in registers (fastest, but limited), in a block or table in memory whose address is passed in a register (used by Linux for many parameters), or pushed on the stack.

Types of system calls with examples:
- Process control: fork(), exec(), exit(), wait(), kill()
- File management: open(), read(), write(), close(), lseek()
- Device management: ioctl(), read(), write() on device files
- Information maintenance: getpid(), time(), alarm(), sleep()
- Communication: pipe(), shmget(), mmap(), socket(), send(), recv()
- Protection: chmod(), chown(), umask()

System call vs function call: a function call stays in user mode and in the program's own address space; a system call crosses into the kernel through a trap, changes the mode, and is much more expensive.

## Interrupts
An interrupt is a signal that makes the CPU stop what it is doing and run an interrupt service routine (ISR).
- Hardware interrupts come from devices (a disk finishing a transfer, a key press, the timer).
- Software interrupts (traps or exceptions) come from the running program: an error such as division by zero or an invalid memory access, or a deliberate system call.

Interrupt handling: the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the program counter and state, looks up the handler address in the interrupt vector (a table of ISR addresses indexed by interrupt number), runs the ISR, then restores the state and continues. Interrupts can be masked (disabled for a short time) and have priorities.

I/O methods: polling (the CPU keeps checking the device: simple but wastes CPU time), interrupt-driven I/O (the device interrupts when ready), and DMA (direct memory access: a controller moves a whole block between device and memory and interrupts once at the end, used for fast devices).

## Common mistakes
- Saying the shell is part of the kernel. It is a user program.
- Confusing a trap (raised by the running program) with a hardware interrupt (raised by a device).
- Thinking a system call is just a library function. The library function only wraps the trap.

## Viva questions
- Why do we need dual-mode operation? To protect the OS and other programs: only the kernel can run privileged instructions.
- What happens when a program calls read()? The wrapper traps into the kernel with the system-call number; the kernel runs sys_read and returns the result.
- Which structure does Linux use? Monolithic with loadable kernel modules.
- Why is a microkernel more reliable? A failing driver or file server runs in user space and can be restarted without crashing the kernel.

# Processes, Threads and Inter-process Communication

## Process concept
A program is a passive file on disk; a process is a program in execution, with its own state. A process in memory has:
- Text section: the program code.
- Data section: global and static variables.
- Heap: memory allocated at run time (malloc, new); it grows upwards.
- Stack: function parameters, return addresses and local variables; it grows downwards.

## Process states
- New: the process is being created.
- Ready: waiting to be assigned the CPU.
- Running: instructions are being executed.
- Waiting (blocked): waiting for an event such as I/O completion.
- Terminated: finished execution.
Transitions: new → ready (admitted), ready → running (scheduler dispatch), running → ready (interrupt or time slice over), running → waiting (I/O or event wait), waiting → ready (I/O or event completion), running → terminated (exit).
source: Processes threads IPC

## Process control block (PCB)
The kernel keeps one PCB per process: process state, process ID, program counter, CPU registers, CPU-scheduling information (priority, queue pointers), memory-management information (base and limit registers, page tables), accounting information (CPU time used), and I/O status (open files, devices).

## Context switch
When the CPU switches from one process to another, the kernel saves the state of the old process in its PCB and loads the saved state of the new one. A context switch is pure overhead: no useful work is done during it. Its time depends on the hardware (number of registers, special instructions).
source: Processes threads IPC

## Operations on processes
- Creation: a parent process creates children, forming a tree of processes (on Linux the root is systemd, PID 1). On UNIX, fork() creates a child that is a copy of the parent; exec() replaces the child's memory with a new program; the parent can call wait() to wait for the child to finish.
- fork() returns 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, and -1 if it fails.
- After n fork() calls in sequence (each executed by every existing process), there are 2^n processes in total, that is 2^n − 1 new processes. Example: three fork() calls give 8 processes.
- Termination: a process calls exit(); the OS frees its resources and reports the exit status to the parent through wait().
- Zombie: a child that has terminated but whose parent has not yet called wait(); its PCB entry stays so the parent can read the status.
- Orphan: a child whose parent terminated first;
source: Processes threads IPC

- Orphan: a child whose parent terminated first; it is adopted by init/systemd, which waits for it.

Modern systems use copy-on-write after fork(): parent and child share pages until one of them writes, so fork() followed by exec() is cheap. Chrome runs each tab in a separate process so one crashing tab does not bring down the browser. Android ranks processes by importance (foreground, visible, service, background, empty) and kills the least important when memory is short.

## Threads
A thread is a basic unit of CPU use inside a process. Threads of the same process share the code, data and open files, but each thread has its own thread ID, program counter, registers and stack.

Benefits: responsiveness (one thread can keep the interface working while another blocks), resource sharing, economy (creating a thread and switching between threads is cheaper than for processes), and scalability on multicore CPUs.

User-level threads are managed by a library without kernel support; kernel-level threads are managed by the OS.

Multithreading models:
- Many-to-one: many user threads on one kernel thread. Cheap, but one blocking system call blocks all threads and they cannot run in parallel on multiple cores.
- One-to-one: each user thread maps to a kernel thread (Linux, Windows). True parallelism; creating many threads costs more.
- Many-to-many: many user threads multiplexed on a smaller or equal number of kernel threads; combines the advantages.

Concurrency means several tasks make progress (possibly by interleaving on one core); parallelism means several tasks run at the same instant on different cores.

Amdahl's law: speedup ≤ 1 / (S + (1 − S) / N), where S is the serial fraction and N the number of cores. Example: with S = 0.25, two cores give at most 1 / (0.25 + 0.375) = 1.6 times speedup, and four cores 1 / (0.25 + 0.1875) ≈ 2.29 times.

Thread libraries: POSIX Pthreads (pthread_create, pthread_join), Windows threads, Java threads. Implicit threading: thread pools, fork-join, OpenMP.

Thread libraries: POSIX Pthreads (pthread_create, pthread_join), Windows threads, Java threads. Implicit threading: thread pools, fork-join, OpenMP.

## Inter-process communication (IPC)
Processes are independent (they do not share data) or cooperating. Cooperating processes need IPC. There are two models:
- Shared memory: the processes share a region of memory and read and write it directly. Fast after setup, because no system call is needed for each access, but the processes must synchronize themselves.
- Message passing: processes exchange messages through the kernel with send() and receive(). Easier to use, no conflicts to manage, and works across machines, but each message costs a system call.
source: Processes threads IPC

## Producer-consumer problem (bounded buffer, shared memory)
A producer creates items and a consumer uses them through a shared circular buffer of size BUFFER_SIZE with two indices: in (next free slot) and out (first full slot).
- Buffer empty: in == out.
- Buffer full: ((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out.
- Producer: while full, wait; buffer[in] = item; in = (in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE.
- Consumer: while empty, wait; item = buffer[out]; out = (out + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE.
With this scheme the buffer holds at most BUFFER_SIZE − 1 items. If a shared counter is used instead, counter++ and counter-- can race, which is why synchronization is needed.
source: Processes threads IPC

## Message passing details
- Direct communication: processes name each other, send(P, message) and receive(Q, message); a link connects exactly one pair.
- Indirect communication: messages go through mailboxes (ports); a link can be shared by several processes.
- Synchronization: blocking (synchronous) send and receive, or non-blocking (asynchronous). Blocking send plus blocking receive is called a rendezvous.
- Buffering: zero capacity (sender must wait for receiver), bounded capacity, unbounded capacity.
- Pipes on UNIX: an ordinary pipe (pipe()) is one-way and used between a parent and child; a named pipe (FIFO) has a name in the file system and can be used by unrelated processes.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking threads of a process have separate data sections. They share them; only the stack and registers are private.
- Counting fork() processes as n + 1 instead of 2^n.
- Saying the circular buffer holds BUFFER_SIZE items; with in/out pointers it holds BUFFER_SIZE − 1.

## Viva questions
- What is stored in a PCB? State, PID, program counter, registers, scheduling, memory and accounting information, open files.
- Difference between a zombie and an orphan? A zombie has finished but is not yet waited for; an orphan is still running but its parent has finished.
- Why are threads cheaper than processes? They share the address space and resources, so creation and switching need less work.
- Shared memory or message passing for large data on one machine? Shared memory, because data is not copied through the kernel for each access.

# Process Synchronization

## Race condition
When several processes or threads access shared data at the same time and the result depends on the order of execution, we have a race condition. Example: counter = 5; the producer executes counter++ and the consumer executes counter-- at the same time. Each is three machine steps (load into a register, add or subtract, store). If they interleave as: producer loads 5, consumer loads 5, producer stores 6, consumer stores 4, the result is 4 instead of 5.

## The critical-section problem
Each process has a critical section, the code that accesses shared data. The structure is: entry section, critical section, exit section, remainder section. A solution must satisfy three requirements:
1. Mutual exclusion: if one process is in its critical section, no other process can be in its critical section.
2. Progress: if no process is in its critical section and some want to enter, only those not in their remainder section take part in deciding who enters next, and the decision cannot be postponed forever.
3. Bounded waiting: there is a limit on how many times other processes can enter their critical sections after a process has asked to enter and before it is allowed in.

## Hardware support
- Disabling interrupts works on a single CPU but not on multiprocessors and is dangerous for user programs.
- test_and_set(&lock): atomically returns the old value of lock and sets it to true. Lock: while (test_and_set(&lock)); unlock: lock = false.
- compare_and_swap(&value, expected, new): atomically sets value to new only if it equals expected, and returns the old value.

## Mutex locks
A mutex lock protects a critical section: acquire() before entering, release() after leaving. A mutex implemented with busy waiting is a spinlock. Spinlocks waste CPU time while waiting, but they avoid a context switch, so they are good on multiprocessors when locks are held for a short time.

## Semaphores
A semaphore S is an integer accessed only through two atomic operations:
- wait(S) (also P): while (S <= 0) wait; S--;
- signal(S) (also V): S++;
A counting semaphore can have any value (for example the number of free buffer slots). A binary semaphore is 0 or 1 and works like a mutex.

Uses:
- Mutual exclusion: semaphore mutex = 1; wait(mutex); critical section; signal(mutex).
- Ordering: to make statement S1 in P1 run before S2 in P2, use synch = 0; P1: S1; signal(synch); P2: wait(synch); S2.

- Ordering: to make statement S1 in P1 run before S2 in P2, use synch = 0; P1: S1; signal(synch); P2: wait(synch); S2.

Implementation without busy waiting: each semaphore has a value and a list of waiting processes. wait() decrements the value and, if it becomes negative, adds the process to the list and blocks it; signal() increments the value and, if it is still ≤ 0, removes a process from the list and wakes it. With this implementation, a negative value −k means k processes are waiting.

Problems: deadlock (P0: wait(S); wait(Q) while P1: wait(Q); wait(S) can wait for each other forever), starvation (a process is never removed from the waiting list, for example with LIFO order), and priority inversion (a low-priority process holds a lock needed by a high-priority one while a medium-priority process runs; solved with priority inheritance).

## Monitors
A monitor is a language construct: a set of procedures and shared data where only one process can be active inside at a time, so mutual exclusion is automatic. Condition variables (x.wait() and x.signal()) let a process wait inside the monitor until a condition becomes true; x.signal() wakes at most one waiting process and does nothing if none is waiting (unlike a semaphore signal, which is remembered).

### Dining-philosophers problem
Five philosophers sit at a round table with one chopstick between each pair; each needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat. If each philosopher does wait(chopstick[i]); wait(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]), all can pick up their left chopstick at once and deadlock. Remedies: allow at most four philosophers at the table, let a philosopher pick up chopsticks only if both are free (inside a critical section or a monitor), or use an asymmetric order (odd philosophers pick up left first, even ones right first).

# Deadlocks

## System model and definition
Processes use resources (CPU cycles, memory, files, I/O devices, locks) in the order request → use → release. A set of processes is deadlocked when every process in the set is waiting for an event (usually the release of a resource) that only another process in the set can cause.

## Necessary conditions (all four must hold at the same time)
1. Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is non-shareable.
2. Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting for more.
3. No preemption: a resource can only be released voluntarily by the process holding it.
4. Circular wait: there is a chain P0 → P1 → ... → Pn → P0 where each process waits for a resource held by the next.

4. Circular wait: there is a chain P0 → P1 → ... → Pn → P0 where each process waits for a resource held by the next.

## Resource-allocation graph (RAG)
Vertices are processes (circles) and resource types (rectangles, with a dot for each instance). A request edge Pi → Rj means Pi is waiting for Rj; an assignment edge Rj → Pi means an instance of Rj is held by Pi.
- No cycle: no deadlock.
- Cycle and every resource has a single instance: deadlock.
- Cycle and some resources have several instances: there may or may not be a deadlock. A cycle is necessary but not sufficient.
A wait-for graph is obtained by removing the resource nodes and joining Pi → Pj when Pi waits for a resource held by Pj. With single-instance resources, a cycle in the wait-for graph means deadlock.

## Methods for handling deadlocks
Prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery, or ignoring the problem (the "ostrich algorithm", used by most general-purpose systems because deadlocks are rare and the other methods are expensive).

## Deadlock prevention (make one condition impossible)
- Mutual exclusion: cannot be removed for non-shareable resources such as printers or locks.
- Hold and wait: request all resources at once before starting, or only when holding none. Low resource utilisation and possible starvation.
- No preemption: if a process holding resources requests one that is not available, it releases everything it holds. Works for resources whose state can be saved (CPU registers, memory), not for printers or locks.
- Circular wait: number all resource types and require requests in increasing order. This is the most practical method.

## Deadlock avoidance: safe states and Banker's algorithm
The OS needs to know in advance the maximum demand of each process. A state is safe if there is a safe sequence <P1, P2, ..., Pn> in which every process can get the resources it still needs from the free resources plus those released by the processes before it. A safe state means no deadlock. An unsafe state does not mean a deadlock has happened; it means the OS can no longer guarantee to avoid one.

Banker's algorithm data structures (n processes, m resource types):
- Available[m]: free instances of each type.
- Max[n][m]: maximum demand of each process.
- Allocation[n][m]: instances currently held.
- Need[n][m] = Max − Allocation.

Safety algorithm (course convention: repeated passes over P0..Pn−1 in order):
1. Work = Available; Finish[i] = false for all i.
2. Find an i with Finish[i] = false and Need[i] ≤ Work (every component).
3. Work = Work + Allocation[i]; Finish[i] = true; go to step 2.
4. If every Finish[i] is true, the state is safe. Any order that passes the check is a valid safe sequence.

Resource-request algorithm for a request by Pi:
1. If Request ≤ Need[i], continue; otherwise it is an error (the process exceeded its maximum claim).
2. If Request ≤ Available, continue; otherwise Pi must wait.
3. Pretend to grant it: Available −= Request, Allocation[i] += Request, Need[i] −= Request. Run the safety algorithm; grant the request only if the new state is safe, otherwise restore the old state and Pi waits.

## Deadlock detection
For single-instance resources, look for a cycle in the wait-for graph. For several instances, use the detection algorithm, which is like the safety algorithm with Request instead of Need:
1. Work = Available; Finish[i] = true if Allocation[i] is all zero, otherwise false.
2. Find i with Finish[i] = false and Request[i] ≤ Work; set Work += Allocation[i], Finish[i] = true; repeat.
3. Every process with Finish[i] = false at the end is deadlocked.
Example: with Allocation P0 (0,1,0), P1 (2,0,0), P2 (3,0,3), P3 (2,1,1), P4 (0,0,2), Request P0 (0,0,0), P1 (2,0,2), P2 (0,0,0), P3 (1,0,0), P4 (0,0,2) and Available (0,0,0), there is no deadlock (order <P0, P2, P3, P4, P1>). If P2 now requests one more C, P1, P2, P3 and P4 are deadlocked.
source: Deadlocks

text:
P4 (0,0,2) and Available (0,0,0), there is no deadlock (order <P0, P2, P3, P4, P1>). If P2 now requests one more C, P1, P2, P3 and P4 are deadlocked.

How often to run detection: every time a request cannot be granted (expensive) or at intervals, for example once an hour or when CPU utilisation drops below 40%.

## Recovery
- Process termination: abort all deadlocked processes (simple but costly), or abort one at a time until the cycle is broken, choosing the victim by priority, time already used, resources held and how many more it needs.
- Resource preemption: select a victim, roll it back to a safe state (or restart it), and make sure the same process is not always the victim (starvation), for example by counting rollbacks in the cost.
source: Deadlocks

text:
to a safe state (or restart it), and make sure the same process is not always the victim (starvation), for example by counting rollbacks in the cost.

## Common mistakes
- Saying unsafe means deadlocked.
- Forgetting to check Request ≤ Need before Request ≤ Available.
- Using Max instead of Need in the safety check.
- Thinking a cycle always means deadlock when resources have several instances.

## Viva questions
- Which prevention method is most practical? Ordering resources to prevent circular wait.
- Why is Banker's algorithm rarely used in general-purpose OSs? Processes rarely know their maximum needs and the check costs O(m × n²) for every request.
- Difference between avoidance and detection? Avoidance never enters an unsafe state; detection lets deadlocks happen and then finds and breaks them.

# Memory Management: Basics, Contiguous Allocation, Paging and Segmentation

## Address binding
Instructions and data can be bound to memory addresses at:
- Compile time: absolute code is generated; the program must be recompiled if its start address changes.
- Load time: relocatable code; addresses are fixed when the program is loaded.
- Execution time: binding is delayed until run time, so the process can be moved in memory during execution. This needs hardware support (an MMU) and is what modern systems use.

## Logical and physical addresses
A logical (virtual) address is generated by the CPU; a physical address is the one seen by the memory unit. With compile-time and load-time binding they are the same; with execution-time binding they differ. The memory-management unit (MMU) maps logical addresses to physical addresses at run time.
source: Memory management

text:
they are the same; with execution-time binding they differ. The memory-management unit (MMU) maps logical addresses to physical addresses at run time.

Relocation and limit registers: the relocation (base) register holds the smallest physical address of the process and the limit register holds the size of its logical address space. Every logical address is first checked: if logical address < limit, physical address = relocation + logical address; otherwise the hardware traps to the OS (addressing error). Example: relocation 14000, limit 3000: logical address 346 → physical 14346; logical address 3500 → trap.
source: Memory management

text:
hardware traps to the OS (addressing error). Example: relocation 14000, limit 3000: logical address 346 → physical 14346; logical address 3500 → trap.

Dynamic loading: a routine is loaded only when it is first called. Dynamic linking: linking to system libraries is postponed until run time (shared libraries, .so or .dll), so one copy in memory is shared by many programs. Swapping: a process can be moved temporarily to a backing store and brought back later; standard swapping of whole processes is slow, so modern systems swap pages, and mobile systems usually avoid swapping.
source: Memory management

text:
g store and brought back later; standard swapping of whole processes is slow, so modern systems swap pages, and mobile systems usually avoid swapping.

## Contiguous memory allocation
Each process occupies one contiguous block of memory.
- Fixed partitions: memory is divided into partitions of fixed size; each holds one process. Leads to internal fragmentation (unused space inside a partition).
- Variable partitions: the OS keeps a list of free blocks (holes) and gives each process a hole of the needed size, splitting the hole. Leads to external fragmentation (enough total free memory, but in pieces that are too small).
source: Memory management

text:
h process a hole of the needed size, splitting the hole. Leads to external fragmentation (enough total free memory, but in pieces that are too small).

Dynamic storage-allocation strategies (course convention: the chosen hole is split and the remainder stays free; next fit resumes its search at the hole used last):
- First fit: the first hole that is big enough. Fast.
- Best fit: the smallest hole that is big enough. Leaves the smallest leftover, but must search the whole list.
- Worst fit: the largest hole. Leaves the largest leftover, which may be useful later; must search the whole list.
- Next fit: like first fit, but starts searching where the previous search ended.
First fit and best fit are better than worst fit in time and storage use; first fit is usually as good as best fit and faster.
source: Memory management

text:

First fit and best fit are better than worst fit in time and storage use; first fit is usually as good as best fit and faster.

## Worked example (solved exactly by OSLLM's solver)
Holes in order: B1 = 100 KB, B2 = 500 KB, B3 = 200 KB, B4 = 300 KB, B5 = 600 KB. Processes in order: P1 = 212 KB, P2 = 417 KB, P3 = 112 KB, P4 = 426 KB.
- First fit: P1 → B2 (288 KB left), P2 → B5 (183 KB left), P3 → B2 (176 KB left), P4 must wait: no hole is 426 KB or larger, even though 959 KB is free in total (external fragmentation).
- Best fit: P1 → B4 (88 left), P2 → B2 (83 left), P3 → B3 (88 left), P4 → B5 (174 left). All four fit.
- Worst fit: P1 → B5 (388 left), P2 → B2 (83 left), P3 → B5 (276 left), P4 must wait.
- Next fit: P1 → B2, P2 → B5, P3 → B5 (search resumes at B5, which still has 183 KB), P4 must wait.
source: Memory management

text:
→ B2 (83 left), P3 → B5 (276 left), P4 must wait.
- Next fit: P1 → B2, P2 → B5, P3 → B5 (search resumes at B5, which still has 183 KB), P4 must wait.

Fragmentation: the 50-percent rule says that with first fit, about N/2 blocks are lost to external fragmentation for N allocated blocks (one third of memory may be unusable). Compaction moves processes together to make one large hole, but it needs execution-time binding and is expensive. Paging and segmentation solve external fragmentation by allowing non-contiguous allocation.

## Paging
Physical memory is divided into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size. Any page can go in any free frame; a page table maps page numbers to frame numbers.
source: Memory management

text:
fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size. Any page can go in any free frame; a page table maps page numbers to frame numbers.

Address translation: with page size 2^n bytes, a logical address is split into page number p = address div 2^n (the high bits) and offset d = address mod 2^n (the low n bits). Physical address = frame(p) × page size + d.
Example: page size 1 KB (1024 bytes) and page table [page 0 → frame 5, page 1 → frame 2, page 2 → frame 7, page 3 → frame 9]. Logical address 3085: p = 3085 div 1024 = 3, d = 3085 − 3072 = 13; frame 9; physical address = 9 × 1024 + 13 = 9229.
source: Memory management

Paging has no external fragmentation, but there is internal fragmentation in the last page of a process (on average half a page). Page-table size: with 32-bit logical addresses and 4 KB pages there are 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 pages; with 4-byte entries the page table is 4 MB per process, which is why multilevel (hierarchical) page tables, hashed page tables and inverted page tables are used. In two-level paging, the page number is split again into an outer index and an inner index.

Protection: each page-table entry has protection bits (read, write, execute) and a valid-invalid bit that marks whether the page is in the process's address space. Shared pages let several processes share one copy of read-only code.
source: Memory management

text:
valid-invalid bit that marks whether the page is in the process's address space. Shared pages let several processes share one copy of read-only code.

## The TLB and effective access time
Every memory access with a page table needs two accesses (page table, then data). A translation look-aside buffer (TLB) is a small, fast associative cache of recent page-table entries.
EAT = h × (TLB time + memory time) + (1 − h) × (TLB time + 2 × memory time), where h is the TLB hit ratio.
Example: memory 100 ns, TLB 20 ns, hit ratio 80%: EAT = 0.8 × 120 + 0.2 × 220 = 96 + 44 = 140 ns. Many textbooks ignore the TLB time: EAT = h × m + (1 − h) × 2m.
source: Memory management

text:
mory 100 ns, TLB 20 ns, hit ratio 80%: EAT = 0.8 × 120 + 0.2 × 220 = 96 + 44 = 140 ns. Many textbooks ignore the TLB time: EAT = h × m + (1 − h) × 2m.

## Segmentation
Segmentation matches the programmer's view: a program is a collection of segments (main program, functions, stack, arrays, symbol table), each with a name and length. A logical address is <segment number, offset>. The segment table holds a base and a limit for each segment; if offset < limit, physical address = base + offset, otherwise trap. Segmentation suffers from external fragmentation; many systems combine segmentation with paging.
source: Memory management

## Common mistakes
- Forgetting to split a hole in variable-partition allocation, or splitting it in fixed partitions.
- Mixing up internal fragmentation (inside an allocated block) and external fragmentation (between blocks).
- Computing the offset with the wrong page size, or forgetting that physical address = frame × page size + offset.
- Counting only one memory access on a TLB miss.

## Viva questions
- Why does paging remove external fragmentation? Any free frame can hold any page, so free memory never has to be contiguous.
- What does the MMU do? Translates logical addresses to physical addresses at run time and checks protection.
- Which allocation strategy is fastest? First fit, because it stops at the first hole that fits.
source: Memory management

# Virtual Memory: Demand Paging, Page Replacement, Thrashing

## Virtual memory
Virtual memory separates the logical memory of a process from physical memory. Only the parts of a program that are needed are in memory, so programs can be larger than physical memory, more programs can run at once, and less I/O is needed to load or swap.

## Demand paging
Pages are loaded only when they are first used (lazy loading). Each page-table entry has a valid-invalid bit: valid means the page is in memory; invalid means it is not in memory (or not part of the address space). Pure demand paging starts a process with no pages in memory.
source: Virtual memory

text:
page is in memory; invalid means it is not in memory (or not part of the address space). Pure demand paging starts a process with no pages in memory.

Page-fault handling:
1. The process references a page whose entry is invalid, and the hardware traps to the OS (page fault).
2. The OS checks an internal table: if the reference is not valid, the process is terminated; if it is valid but not in memory, the page must be brought in.
3. Find a free frame (or choose a victim with a page-replacement algorithm).
4. Schedule a disk read of the page into the frame.
5. When the read finishes, update the page table (valid) and the internal table.
6. Restart the instruction that caused the fault.
source: Virtual memory

text:

5. When the read finishes, update the page table (valid) and the internal table.
6. Restart the instruction that caused the fault.

Effective access time with page faults: EAT = (1 − p) × memory access time + p × page-fault service time, where p is the page-fault rate.
Example: memory access 200 ns, fault service time 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns. With p = 1/1000: EAT = 0.999 × 200 + 0.001 × 8,000,000 = 199.8 + 8000 = 8199.8 ns, about 8.2 microseconds, a slowdown of about 40 times. To keep the slowdown under 10% (EAT < 220 ns) we need 220 > 200 + 7,999,800 × p, so p < 0.0000025: fewer than one fault in about 400,000 accesses.

Copy-on-write: after fork(), parent and child share pages marked copy-on-write; a page is copied only when one of them writes to it.

Copy-on-write: after fork(), parent and child share pages marked copy-on-write; a page is copied only when one of them writes to it.

## Page replacement
When a page fault occurs and no frame is free, the OS chooses a victim frame, writes it to disk if it has been modified (dirty bit set), reads in the new page and restarts the process. Algorithms are compared by the number of page faults on a reference string.
source: Virtual memory

text:
modified (dirty bit set), reads in the new page and restarts the process. Algorithms are compared by the number of page faults on a reference string.

- FIFO: replace the page that has been in memory the longest. Simple, but it can replace heavily used pages, and it suffers from Belady's anomaly.
- Optimal (OPT): replace the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It gives the lowest possible number of faults, but needs future knowledge, so it is used as a benchmark. (Course convention: among pages never used again, the one loaded earliest is replaced.)
- LRU (least recently used): replace the page that has not been used for the longest time. A good approximation of OPT; implemented with counters (time of last use) or a stack of page numbers, or approximated in hardware.

## Worked example (solved exactly by OSLLM's solver)
Reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames:
- FIFO: 15 page faults, 5 hits. Frames after each reference: 7-- | 70- | 701 | 201 | 201 | 231 | 230 | 430 | 420 | 423 | 023 | 023 | 023 | 013 | 012 | 012 | 012 | 712 | 702 | 701.
- LRU: 12 page faults, 8 hits. Frames: 7-- | 70- | 701 | 201 | 201 | 203 | 203 | 403 | 402 | 432 | 032 | 032 | 032 | 132 | 132 | 102 | 102 | 107 | 107 | 107.
- OPT: 9 page faults, 11 hits. Frames: 7-- | 70- | 701 | 201 | 201 | 203 | 203 | 243 | 243 | 243 | 203 | 203 | 203 | 201 | 201 | 201 | 201 | 701 | 701 | 701.
Hit ratio = hits ÷ references; for LRU 8/20 = 40%.

Hit ratio = hits ÷ references; for LRU 8/20 = 40%.

## Belady's anomaly
With FIFO, adding frames can increase the number of page faults. Reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5: FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4 frames. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms (the pages in memory with n frames are always a subset of those with n + 1 frames), so they never show Belady's anomaly.
source: Virtual memory

## LRU approximations
- Reference bit: set by hardware when a page is used; the OS clears it periodically.
- Second-chance (clock) algorithm: FIFO order in a circular list; if the victim's reference bit is 1, clear it, give the page a second chance and move on; replace the first page found with reference bit 0.
- Counting algorithms: LFU (least frequently used) and MFU (most frequently used); not common.
source: Virtual memory

- Counting algorithms: LFU (least frequently used) and MFU (most frequently used); not common.

## Frame allocation
- Equal allocation: m frames among n processes, m/n each.
- Proportional allocation: a_i = (s_i / S) × m, where s_i is the size of process i and S the total. Example: 62 frames, processes of 10 and 127 pages: 10/137 × 62 ≈ 4 frames and 127/137 × 62 ≈ 57 frames.
- Global replacement: a process may take a frame from any process (better throughput, but a process cannot control its own fault rate). Local replacement: only from its own frames.
source: Virtual memory

text:
s may take a frame from any process (better throughput, but a process cannot control its own fault rate). Local replacement: only from its own frames.

## Thrashing
A process is thrashing when it spends more time paging than executing. Cause: the processes do not have enough frames for the pages they are actively using, so they fault constantly. The OS sees low CPU utilisation, adds more processes, which makes it worse; CPU utilisation collapses as the degree of multiprogramming rises.

Locality model: a process moves from one locality (a set of pages used together) to another. Thrashing happens when the total size of the current localities is larger than memory.
source: Virtual memory

text:
es from one locality (a set of pages used together) to another. Thrashing happens when the total size of the current localities is larger than memory.

Working-set model: the working set WS(t, Δ) is the set of pages referenced in the last Δ references (the working-set window). Let D = Σ WSS_i be the total demand. If D > m (available frames), thrashing will occur, so the OS suspends a process. Example: with Δ = 10 and the last ten references 1 2 1 5 7 7 7 7 5 1, the working set is {1, 2, 5, 7}, so WSS = 4.

Page-fault frequency (PFF): set an upper and a lower bound on the fault rate; if a process faults too often, give it more frames; if too rarely, take frames away.
source: Virtual memory

requency (PFF): set an upper and a lower bound on the fault rate; if a process faults too often, give it more frames; if too rarely, take frames away.

## Common mistakes
- In OPT, looking backwards instead of forwards in the reference string.
- In LRU, using the time a page was loaded instead of the time it was last used (that would be FIFO).
- Counting the first loads into empty frames as hits. They are page faults.
- Thinking more frames always means fewer faults. Not for FIFO (Belady's anomaly).

## Viva questions
- Why is OPT not used in practice? It needs to know the future reference string.
- What causes thrashing and how is it controlled? Too few frames for the active localities; control it with the working-set model or page-fault frequency and by reducing multiprogramming.
- What is the dirty bit for? To avoid writing a page back to disk if it was not modified.
source: Virtual memory

# File Systems and Disk Scheduling

## File concept
A file is a named collection of related information stored on secondary storage. Attributes: name, identifier, type, location, size, protection, timestamps and owner. Operations: create, open, read, write, reposition (seek), delete, truncate, close. The OS keeps an open-file table with the file pointer, open count, location and access rights.

## Access methods
- Sequential access: records are read in order (like a tape); read_next and write_next.
- Direct (relative) access: any block can be read or written by number; used by databases.
- Indexed access: an index file holds pointers to blocks; search the index, then go directly to the block.
source: File systems and disk scheduling

- Indexed access: an index file holds pointers to blocks; search the index, then go directly to the block.

## Directory structures
- Single-level: one directory for all users; name clashes.
- Two-level: a separate directory for each user.
- Tree-structured: directories inside directories; absolute and relative path names.
- Acyclic graph: files and subdirectories can be shared through links; deletion needs care (dangling pointers, reference counts).
- General graph: allows cycles; needs garbage collection.
source: File systems and disk scheduling

ries can be shared through links; deletion needs care (dangling pointers, reference counts).
- General graph: allows cycles; needs garbage collection.

## Allocation methods
- Contiguous: each file occupies consecutive blocks; the directory stores the start and length. Supports sequential and direct access and is fast, but suffers external fragmentation and files are hard to grow.
- Linked: each block points to the next; the directory stores the first and last block. No external fragmentation and files grow easily, but direct access is slow and a damaged pointer loses the rest of the file. FAT (file-allocation table) keeps all the links in one table at the start of the disk.
- Indexed: each file has an index block holding the addresses of all its blocks (UNIX inode). Supports direct access without external fragmentation; costs an index block per file. Large files use linked index blocks or multilevel indexes.
source: File systems and disk scheduling

UNIX inode: 12 direct block pointers, one single indirect, one double indirect and one triple indirect pointer. With 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers, one block holds 1024 pointers, so the maximum file size is 12 × 4 KB + 1024 × 4 KB + 1024² × 4 KB + 1024³ × 4 KB = 48 KB + 4 MB + 4 GB + 4 TB, about 4 TB.

Hard link vs soft link: a hard link is another directory entry pointing to the same inode (the file is deleted only when the link count reaches 0; cannot cross file systems). A soft (symbolic) link is a separate small file holding a path name; it breaks if the target is deleted.

## Free-space management
- Bit vector (bitmap): one bit per block (1 = free). Easy to find contiguous free blocks; for a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks it needs 2^28 bits = 32 MB.
- Linked list: free blocks linked together; no wasted space but slow to traverse.
- Grouping: the first free block stores the addresses of n free blocks.
- Counting: store the address of the first free block and the number of free blocks that follow it.
source: File systems and disk scheduling

free block stores the addresses of n free blocks.

## Disk structure and access time
A hard disk has platters with tracks; the tracks at one arm position form a cylinder; tracks are divided into sectors. Access time = seek time (moving the head to the cylinder) + rotational latency (waiting for the sector to come under the head) + transfer time. Seek time is the largest part, and disk scheduling tries to reduce the total head movement.

## Disk scheduling algorithms
Course conventions: SSTF ties go to the request that comes first in the queue; SCAN and C-SCAN travel to the edge of the disk; the return jump of C-SCAN and C-LOOK is counted in the total head movement.
- FCFS: serve requests in arrival order. Fair, but can swing the head wildly.
- SSTF (shortest seek time first): always serve the closest pending request. Much less movement, but requests far from the head can starve; it is not always optimal.
- SCAN (elevator): move in one direction serving requests until the end of the disk, then reverse.
- C-SCAN (circular SCAN): move in one direction to the end, jump back to the other end, and continue in the same direction. Gives a more uniform waiting time.
- LOOK: like SCAN, but reverse at the last request in that direction instead of going to the edge.
- C-LOOK: like C-SCAN, but go only as far as the last request and

- C-LOOK: like C-SCAN, but go only as far as the last request and jump back to the farthest request on the other side.

Choosing an algorithm: SSTF is common and simple; SCAN and C-SCAN perform better under heavy load and avoid starvation; with SSDs there is no seek, so FCFS (or a simple merging queue) is used.

## Common mistakes
- Forgetting the move to the edge of the disk in SCAN and C-SCAN.
- Leaving out (or adding, against the course convention) the return jump in C-SCAN and C-LOOK.

## Permissions
Each file has read (r = 4), write (w = 2) and execute (x = 1) permissions for the user (owner), group and others. ls -l shows them as, for example, -rwxr-xr--.
- chmod 754 file: rwx for the owner (7 = 4 + 2 + 1), r-x for the group (5 = 4 + 1), r-- for others (4).
- chmod u+x file, chmod go-w file: symbolic form (u user, g group, o others, a all; + add, - remove, = set).
- chown user:group file: change the owner and group. umask sets default permissions for new files.

## Processes
- ps: list processes; ps -ef or ps aux shows all processes with PID, parent PID, CPU and memory use.
- top (or htop): live view of processes and CPU use.
- kill PID: send SIGTERM (polite termination); kill -9 PID: send SIGKILL, which cannot be caught or ignored. killall name kills by name.
- command &: run in the background; jobs lists background jobs; fg %1 and bg %1 move job 1 to the foreground or background; Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job; Ctrl+C sends SIGINT.
- nice -n 10 command: start with lower priority (nice values -20 highest to 19 lowest); renice changes a running process.
- pstree shows the process tree.

## Archives, disks and system information
- tar -cvf archive.tar dir (create), tar -xvf archive.tar (extract), tar -czvf archive.tar.gz dir (create compressed).
- gzip file / gunzip file.gz; zcat file.gz shows a compressed file without extracting.

- free -h: memory usage. uname -a: kernel and system information. who, whoami, w: logged-in users. date, cal: date and calendar. uptime: running time and load.
- passwd: change your password. sudo command: run as administrator. man command: the manual page; command --help: short help.
- ssh user@host: remote login; scp copies files over ssh; ping host and host name check the network.

## Pipes and redirection
- command > file: write standard output to a file (overwrite); >> appends.
- command < file: read standard input from a file.
- command 2> file: redirect error messages; command > file 2>&1 sends both output and errors to the file.
- cmd1 | cmd2: a pipe sends the output of cmd1 to the input of cmd2. Each command runs as a separate process connected by a pipe created with the pipe() system call.
Examples: ls -l | wc -l (count entries), ps aux | grep firefox (find a process), cat words.txt | tr ' ' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head (most common words).

## Common mistakes
- Using rm -r without checking the path; deleted files cannot be recovered.
- Reading chmod digits in the wrong order: the first digit is the owner, then group, then others.
- Expecting kill to stop every process; a process can catch SIGTERM, but not SIGKILL.

## Viva questions
- What does chmod 640 give? rw- for the owner, r-- for the group, nothing for others.
- Difference between > and >>? > overwrites the file; >> appends to it.
- How do ps and top get their information? From the /proc file system maintained by the kernel.

# Interlude: Process API (Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces)

Interlude: Process API

ASIDE: INTERLUDES Interludes will cover more practical aspects of systems, including a particular focus on operating system APIs and how to use them. If you don’t like practical things, you could skip these interludes. But you should like practical things, because, well, they are generally useful in real life; companies, for example, don’t usually hire you for your non-practical skills.

In this interlude, we discuss process creation in UNIX systems. UNIX presents one of the most intriguing ways to create a new process with a pair of system calls: fork() and exec(). A third routine, wait(), can be used by a process wishing to wait for a process it has created to complete. We now present these interfaces in more detail, with a few simple examples to motivate us. And thus, our problem:
source: Interlude: Process API (Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces)

5.1 The fork() System Call

The fork() system call is used to create a new process [C63]. However, be forewarned: it is certainly the strangest routine you will ever call1. More speciﬁcally, you have a running program whose code looks like what you see in Figure 5.1; examine the code, or better yet, type it in and run it yourself!

Now the interesting part begins. The process calls the fork() system call, which the OS provides as a way to create a new process. The odd part: the process that is created is an (almost) exact copy of the calling process. That means that to the OS, it now looks like there are two copies of the program p1 running, and both are about to return from the fork() system call. The newly-created process (called the child, in contrast to the creating parent) doesn’t start running at main(), like you might expect (note, the “hello” message only got printed out once); rather, it just comes into life as if it had called fork() itself.

So far, we haven’t done much: just created a child that prints out a message and exits. Sometimes, as it turns out, it is quite useful for a parent to wait for a child process to ﬁnish what it has been doing. This task is accomplished with the wait() system call (or its more complete sibling waitpid()); see Figure 5.2 for details.

In this example (p2.c), the parent process calls wait() to block (i.e., delay its execution) until the child ﬁnishes executing. When the child is done, the parent becomes unblocked, and wait() returns in the parent.

With this code, we now know that the child will always print ﬁrst. Why do we know that? Well, it might simply run ﬁrst, as before, and thus print before the parent. However, if the parent does happen to run ﬁrst, it will immediately call wait(); this system call won’t return until the child has run and exited2. Thus, even when the parent runs ﬁrst, it politely waits for the child to ﬁnish running, then wait() returns, and then the parent prints its message.

5.4 Why? Motivating The API

Of course, one big question you might have: why would we build such an odd interface to what should be the simple act of creating a new process? Well, as it turns out, the separation of fork() and exec() is essential in building a UNIX shell, because it lets the shell run code after the call to fork() but before the call to exec(); this code can alter the environment of the about-to-be-run program, and thus enables a variety of interesting features to be readily built.

The shell is just a user program4. It shows you a prompt and then waits for you to type something into it. You then type a command (i.e., the name of an executable program, plus any arguments) into it; in most cases, the shell then ﬁgures out where in the ﬁle system the executable resides, calls fork() to create a new child process to run the command, calls some variant of exec() to run the command, and then waits for the command to complete by calling wait(). When the child completes, the shell returns from wait() and prints out a prompt again, ready for your next command.

The separation of fork() and exec() allows the shell to do a whole bunch of useful things rather easily. For example:

prompt> wc p3.c > newfile.txt

The way the shell accomplishes this task is quite simple: when the child is created, before calling exec(), the shell (speciﬁcally, the code executed in the child process) closes standard output and opens the ﬁle newfile.txt. By doing so, any output from the soonto-be-running program wc is sent to the ﬁle instead of the screen (open ﬁle descriptors are kept open across the exec() call, thus enabling this behavior [SR05]).

Subsequent writes by the child process to the standard output ﬁle descriptor, for example by routines such as printf(), will then be routed transparently to the newly-opened ﬁle instead of the screen.
